title: PPO Series 1: The Policy Gradient Theorem
text:
InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022), a direct precursor to ChatGPT’s RLHF methodology, used Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al. 2017) with a KL-to-reference constraint to perform online policy optimization against a preference-trained reward model. PPO has since become a cornerstone of the GenAI era.
PPO is a policy-gradient method that updates a parameterized policy via stochastic gradient ascent to increase expected reward, but it is engineered to avoid the dominant failure mode of vanilla policy gradients: overly large steps that induce policy drift and abrupt performance collapse under noisy advantage estimates and scarce on-policy data. Its “proximal” idea is to constrain each update so the new policy cannot move too far from the old policy on sampled actions, keeping improvements incremental and reliable.
But to truly grasp how PPO calculates these updates and why it requires constraints, we must first understand the mathematical engine driving it: the fundamental Policy Gradient Theorem.
The Policy Gradient Theorem involves a lot of moving parts. Before we dive into the derivations, keep this notation glossary handy to help you track the variables, spaces, and probability distributions.


Notation Glossary (Click to expand)










Notation

\mathcal{S}
The state space (the set of all possible states in the environment).


\mathcal{A}
The action space (the set of all possible actions the agent can take).


s, s', s''
Specific, concrete states within the environment.


S_t
A random variable representing the state at a specific time step t.


s_t
A specific, observed state value at time step t in a sample.


s_0, S_0
The initial state (s_0 as a concrete value, S_0 as a random variable).


a
A specific action taken by the agent.


t
A discrete time step in the environment.


\tau
A realized trajectory or sampled sequence of interactions: \{s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, \dots\}.













Notation
Description




\theta
The learnable parameters of the neural network (or function approximator) defining the policy.


V^\pi(s)
The state-value function; the expected return starting from state s and following policy \pi.


Q^\pi(s, a)
The action-value function; the expected return starting from state s, taking action a, and then following policy \pi.


r(s, a)
The immediate reward received by the agent after taking action a in state s.


J(\theta)
The overall objective function to be maximized (the expected return of the policy).


\phi(s)
The local policy improvement term at state s, defined as the sum of policy gradients weighted by action-values.













Notation
Description




\pi
The policy followed by the agent.


\pi(a \mid s)
The probability of taking action a when in state s, according to policy \pi.


P(s' \mid s, a)
The environment’s transition probability of moving to state s' after taking action a in state s. This is the transition model (or system dynamics) of the Markov Decision Process (MDP). It belongs entirely to the environment and has absolutely nothing to do with the agent’s policy.


P(s \to s')
The transition probability of moving from state s to s' under the current behavior of policy \pi. This is the state-to-state transition probability under a specific policy \pi. It combines the agent’s decision-making with the environment’s physics.


\mu_0(s_0)
The probability distribution of the starting state s_0.


\mu_\pi(s)
The discounted state visitation distribution (or unnormalized frequency) indicating how much time the agent spends in state s under policy \pi.


\text{Pr}(S_t = s \mid s_0, \pi)
The exact probability of the agent being in state s at time step t, given it started at s_0 and follows policy \pi.

title: PPO Series 1: The Policy Gradient Theorem
text:
2 Bellman Equation
The Bellman Equation (Sutton and Barto 2018) for the state-value function V^\pi(s) is the expected value of all possible actions taken from that state:
V^\pi(s) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a|s) Q^\pi(s, a)
When we apply the gradient operator \nabla_\theta to both sides of this equation, we use the product rule (Leibniz rule) because both the policy \pi(a|s) and the action-value function Q^\pi(s, a) are functions of the policy parameters \theta:
\nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \left[ \nabla_{\theta} \pi(a|s) Q^{\pi}(s, a) + \pi(a|s) \nabla_{\theta} Q^{\pi}(s, a) \right] \tag{1}
The Bellman equation for the action-value function Q^\pi(s, a) is:
Q^{\pi}(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} P(s'|s, a) V^{\pi}(s')
This equation defines the value of taking a specific action a in state s as the immediate reward r(s, a) plus the discounted expected value of the resulting next state s'. When we apply the gradient operator \nabla_{\theta} to this expression, the immediate reward r(s, a) and the environment’s transition probabilities P(s'|s, a) are treated as constants because they do not depend on the policy parameters \theta.
Consequently, the gradient passes through the summation and the transition model, focusing entirely on the change in the future state-value function \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s'):
\nabla_{\theta} Q^{\pi}(s, a) = \nabla_{\theta} \left( r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} P(s'|s, a) V^{\pi}(s') \right) = \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} P(s'|s, a) \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s') \tag{2}
Substituting Equation 2 back into the original expression Equation 1 reveals a recursive structure:
\nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s) = \underbrace{\sum_{a} \nabla_{\theta} \pi(a|s) Q^{\pi}(s, a)}_{\phi(s)} + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s \to s') \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s') \tag{3} Here, P(s \to s') represents the transition probability from state s to s' under the current policy \pi. Replace the \nabla_\theta V^\pi(s') on the right side with its own definition Equation 3, we have: \nabla_\theta V^\pi(s) = \phi(s) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s \to s') \left[ \phi(s') + \gamma \sum_{s''} P(s' \to s'') \nabla_\theta V^\pi(s'') \right] By distributing the transition probability across the terms of the recursive expansion, the relationship between the state-space summations and the time-indexed expectations becomes clear:
\nabla_\theta V^\pi(s) = \phi(s) + \gamma \underbrace{\sum_{s'} P(s \to s') \phi(s')}_{\mathbb{E}_\pi[\phi(S_1) \mid s]} + \gamma^2 \underbrace{\sum_{s'} \sum_{s''} P(s \to s') P(s' \to s'') \phi(s'')}_{\mathbb{E}_\pi[\phi(S_2) \mid s]} + \dots \tag{4}
This expansion demonstrates how the value function gradient at state s is constructed from the immediate local improvement and the discounted sum of expected future improvements. The terms under the brackets identify that the summation over all possible next states s' is the mathematical definition of the expectation over the random variable S_1, while the nested summation over s'' represents the expectation over S_2. By viewing the derivation this way, it is evident that the gradient at any single point is a cumulative measure of all potential future policy updates along every possible path the agent might take.

Side note: To calculate P(s \to s'), you have to sum up the probabilities of every possible action the agent could take in state s, multiplied by the environment’s probability of moving to s' given that specific action. Mathematically, P(s \to s') is the marginalization of P(s' \mid s, a) over the policy \pi:
P(s \to s') = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a \mid s) P(s' \mid s, a) This shows exactly why P(s \to s') shifts whenever you update the policy parameters \theta, whereas P(s' \mid s, a) remains rigidly fixed for the entire training process!

title: PPO Series 1: The Policy Gradient Theorem
section: 3 From a Time-based View to a State-based View
text:
3 From a Time-based View to a State-based View
The core “magic” of the policy gradient theorem is the conceptual shift from tracking an agent’s individual steps through time (t=0, 1, 2, \dots) to observing the aggregate density of the agent’s presence across the environment’s state space (s \in \mathcal{S}). It proves that we do not need to calculate an infinite series of future effects for every specific moment in time. Instead, we can simply look at the global state visitation distribution \mu_\pi(s)—the state-based view—to determine how to update our policy parameters \theta.
The time-based view (forward perspective) describes the gradient as the expected sum of all future local policy “nudges” \phi(S_t), discounted by \gamma^t, starting from the initial state s_0. It focuses on the sequential trajectory of the agent.
The state-based view (stationary perspective) collapses the time dimension into the stationary distribution \mu_\pi(s). It treats the gradient as a simple weighted average of the local improvements \phi(s) over the entire state space, which is what allows us to train using a buffer of sampled transitions.
To clarify the notation, we use S_t (uppercase) for the random variable and s_t (lowercase) for the specific value observed in a sample. The sampled sequence is a realized trajectory \tau = \{s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, \dots\}.

3.1 The Time-based View
The goal of the agent is to maximize its expected return from the moment it begins interacting with the environment. We formally define this objective function J(\theta) as the expected value of the state-value function over the initial state distribution:
J(\theta) \triangleq \mathbb{E}_{s_0 \sim \mu_0}[V^\pi(s_0)]
Writing this expectation explicitly as a sum over all possible initial states s_0, weighted by their starting probability \mu_0(s_0), gives us the starting point for our derivation:
J(\theta) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) V^{\pi}(s_0) Before moving further, it is worth pausing to clarify the notation \mu_0. The subscript 0 explicitly refers to the time step t=0, denoting the environment’s initial state distribution. This distinction is necessary because the very first state an agent encounters is typically determined entirely by the environment’s reset mechanics, independent of the agent’s behavior. We use the 0 subscript to isolate this localized starting point from the subsequent trajectory. This directly contrasts with \mu_\pi(s), which appears in the state-based view (stationary perspective). While \mu_0 only captures the isolated snapshot at the exact moment an episode begins, \mu_\pi(s) is the discounted state visitation distribution that aggregates the probability of visiting a state across all future time steps (t=0, 1, 2, \dots). Unlike the starting state, this global distribution is continuously shaped by the agent’s active policy \pi.
We begin with the gradient of the objective J(\theta), which is the weighted sum of the gradients of the values of the initial states s_0: \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s_0) As established in the recursive unrolling of the Bellman equation in Equation 4, \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s_0) is equal to the discounted sum of all future local policy improvements \phi(\cdot) that the agent will encounter: \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \left[ \phi(s_0) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\phi(S_1) \mid s_0] + \gamma^2 \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\phi(S_2) \mid s_0] + \dots \right] Note that s_0 is the specific value we are summing over. S_1 is the random variable (the unknown future). We are iterating through every possible concrete state in the state space \mathcal{S} and weighting the result by the probability \mu_0(s_0). When we are “inside” a summation, we are usually dealing with a specific, fixed value for that iteration.However, the starting point of the process, considered as a concept, is a random variable S_0.


3.2 The State-based View
To see how the “collapse” happens, we write out the expectations as explicit sums over all possible states s that could be visited at each time step t:
\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \sum_{s} \text{Pr}(S_t = s \mid s_0, \pi) \phi(s)
The mathematical “miracle” occurs when we swap the order of the summations for t and s. Instead of tracking what happens at each second of the agent’s life, we look at each state s in the environment and ask how much total discounted weight it accumulates across all possible times: \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s} \left[ \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \text{Pr}(S_t = s \mid s_0, \pi) \right] \phi(s) \tag{5} The expression inside the brackets is exactly the definition of the discounted state visitation distribution \mu_\pi(s). It represents the total discounted probability of visiting state s over an infinite horizon, given the starting distribution \mu_0 and the behavior of policy \pi: \mu_\pi(s) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \text{Pr}(S_t = s \mid s_0, \pi) In the formula, S_t is the random variable representing the state at time t, and the sum over s_0 accounts for the probability of starting in various initial states according to the distribution \mu_0. This expression represents the unnormalized discounted state visitation frequency, which measures the total expected discounted time an agent spends in state s over an infinite horizon. Unlike a standard probability distribution that sums to one, the sum of this measure over the entire state space \mathcal{S} equals 1/(1-\gamma), reflecting the total discounted time available in the process. When using this unnormalized form in the policy gradient theorem, the gradient \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) is expressed as a direct sum \sum_{s} \mu_{\pi}(s) \phi(s), effectively accumulating every local policy improvement throughout the agent’s lifetime. If a normalized probability distribution is required for an expectation, this frequency is typically multiplied by (1-\gamma) to ensure the weights sum to unity.
By substituting \mu_\pi(s) back into Equation 5, the infinite time series collapses into a single, elegant spatial weighting: \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s} \mu_\pi(s) \phi(s) \tag{6}
This result is fundamental because it proves that the complex, indirect effect of the policy on the future state distribution is already captured by simply weighting the local gradients by the current visitation frequency. We do not need to compute the derivative of the distribution itself; we only need to sample from it. As established in the recursive unrolling, the total gradient of the objective J(\theta) is the sum of these local improvements across all states, weighted by the discounted visitation frequency \mu_\pi(s).

The policy gradient theorem establishes that

However, this shortcut only holds true for the exact gradient at the current 	heta; as soon as the policy moves too far, the old distribution \mu_{\pi_{old}}(s) no longer matches the new reality, causing the gradient estimate to become unreliable. Understanding this limitation naturally leads to the next question: how can we update policies while ensuring the new policy does not drift too far from the old one? This question motivates Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO), which we explore in the next post: PPO Series 2: Trust Region Policy Optimization.

title: PPO Series 2: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) (Schulman et al. 2017) is a policy-based reinforcement learning method that shares the same fundamental objective function as standard policy gradient algorithms: maximizing the expected value J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_S[V_\pi(S)].
As shown by the Policy Gradient Theorem (see my previous post PPO Series 1: The Policy Gradient Theorem), this objective can be optimized by estimating the gradient of J(\theta) with respect to the policy parameters. Importantly, TRPO does not change this objective; instead, it modifies how the policy update is performed by constraining how far the new policy can move from the old one. While standard policy gradient algorithms rely on stochastic gradient ascent to improve the policy, TRPO utilizes a trust-region algorithm. This approach ensures more stable and reliable updates by constraining how much the policy can change in a single step, helping to prevent the performance collapses often seen with traditional gradient methods.

title: PPO Series 2: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
1 Trust Region Optimization
At its core, Trust Region optimization is a strategy for safely navigating complex, non-linear objective functions f(x) by relying on bounded local approximations. Instead of picking a direction and then guessing a step size like standard line search methods, trust region methods first define a safe maximum step distance, and then find the optimal update within that strict boundary.
The algorithm proceeds in three main phases:

The Local Approximation
At the current parameter state x_k, we construct a simplified local model of the landscape, typically a second-order Taylor expansion denoted as m_k(p), where p is the proposed step vector. We mathematically “trust” this approximation is accurate only within a specific radius, \Delta_k.
The Constrained Subproblem
We find the optimal step p by minimizing the local model subject to the trust-region boundary constraint:
Minimize: m_k(p)
Subject to: \|p\| \le \Delta_k
The Dynamic Evaluation
Before officially updating the parameters, we measure how well our local model predicted the actual landscape. We calculate the agreement ratio \rho_k, which compares the actual reduction in the true objective function to the predicted reduction from our simplified model:
\rho_k = \frac{f(x_k) - f(x_k + p_k)}{m_k(0) - m_k(p_k)}

Based on \rho_k, the algorithm dynamically adjusts. If \rho_k is close to 1, the model is highly accurate; the step is accepted, and the trust region \Delta_k is expanded for faster optimization. If \rho_k is negative, the model was wrong and the step actually made things worse; the step is rejected, the trust region is shrunk, and the algorithm tries again within a tighter, safer boundary. This feedback loop guarantees stable, monotonic improvement even in highly unpredictable loss landscapes.

title: PPO Series 2: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
2 Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO)

2.1 The Surrogate Objective
Policy Gradient Theorem proves that the gradient of the state distribution does not affect the policy gradient at the current parameters \theta, it saves us from modeling the environment’s transition dynamics. This shortcut only holds true for the exact gradient at the current \theta. This is exactly why TRPO cannot just use J(\theta) and must rely on the surrogate objective L(\theta).
Instead of directly maximizing the expected return J(\theta), TRPO optimizes a surrogate objective function. Let \theta_{old} be the parameters of the current policy and \theta be the parameters of the proposed new policy. TRPO seeks to maximize the following expected advantage:
L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
In this equation, A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) is the advantage function, which measures how much better a specific action is compared to the average baseline action in a given state. The ratio \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} tracks how the probability of taking that action changes under the new policy.
It was proved that the true objective J(\theta) is mathematically guaranteed to improve as long as L(\theta) improves and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the old and new policies is strictly penalized (Schulman et al. 2017) . By enforcing a hard constraint on this KL divergence, TRPO traps the optimization step inside a safe, narrow boundary where L(\theta) remains a valid and reliable proxy for J(\theta).


2.2 The KL Divergence Constraint
To prevent the catastrophic updates mentioned earlier, TRPO restricts the change in the policy using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, a mathematical statistic that measures how one probability distribution differs from a second, reference probability distribution.
Rather than just adding a penalty to the objective function, TRPO enforces a hard constraint on the average KL divergence over the state space. The formal constrained optimization problem is written as:
Maximize:
L(\theta) \tag{1}
Subject to:
\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s)) \right] \le \delta
The parameter \delta is a predefined, small scalar value that defines the maximum allowed KL divergence. This creates the “trust region” around the current policy. By enforcing this boundary, the algorithm mathematically guarantees that the new policy \pi_{\theta} will not diverge significantly from \pi_{\theta_{old}} for any given state. Because the policy is only allowed to change within this safe, trusted region, TRPO maintains stable and theoretically guaranteed monotonic improvement during the learning process.


2.3 Local Approximation using Taylor Expansion
Let the change in policy parameters be \Delta \theta = \theta - \theta_{old}.
First, we approximate the objective function L(\theta) using a first-order Taylor expansion around \theta_{old}:
L(\theta) \approx L(\theta_{old}) + g^T \Delta \theta
Here, g is the policy gradient evaluated at \theta_{old}:
g = \nabla_{\theta} L(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}}
Second, we approximate the KL divergence constraint using a second-order Taylor expansion. The zeroth and first-order terms of the KL divergence between identical distributions are zero, leaving only the second-order term. The detailed proof is provided in Section 4.
\bar{D}_{KL}(\theta_{old}, \theta) \approx \frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T H \Delta \theta
Here, H is the Hessian matrix of the KL divergence. In the context of probability distributions, this Hessian is equivalent to the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), as shown in Section 5.
\bar{D}_{KL}(\theta_{old}, \theta) is a shorthand convention used heavily in the actual TRPO paper to make the equations readable. The bar on top denotes a mean or expectation. It specifically represents the average KL divergence over all the states actually sampled in the rollout buffer. Mathematically, it is defined as: \bar{D}_{KL}(\theta_{old}, \theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_\theta(\cdot|s)) \right] D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_\theta(\cdot|s)) is the exact, formal application of that concept to our policy networks. It represents the KL divergence between the old policy and the new policy at one single, specific state s.
By substituting these approximations back into the original TRPO formulation Equation 1, the problem simplifies into a quadratic program:
Maximize:
g^T \Delta \theta
Subject to:
\frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T H \Delta \theta \le \delta
To find the optimal step direction and size, we construct the Lagrangian for this constrained problem:
\mathcal{L}(\Delta \theta, \lambda) = g^T \Delta \theta - \lambda \left( \frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T H \Delta \theta - \delta \right)
We find the maximum by taking the derivative with respect to \Delta \theta and setting it to zero:
\nabla_{\Delta \theta} \mathcal{L} = g - \lambda H \Delta \theta = 0
\Delta \theta = \frac{1}{\lambda} H^{-1} g
This gives us the optimal update direction. Let the search direction be x = H^{-1} g. To find the scalar \lambda, we plug \Delta \theta back into the constraint boundary equation:
\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{\lambda} x \right)^T H \left( \frac{1}{\lambda} x \right) = \delta
\frac{1}{2 \lambda^2} x^T H x = \delta
\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{x^T H x}{2\delta}}
Finally, substituting \lambda back into the equation for \Delta \theta gives the exact parameter update:
\Delta \theta = \sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{x^T H x}} x


2.4 Bypassing the Matrix Inversion with Conjugate Gradient
The equation above requires computing x = H^{-1} g, which is equivalent to solving the linear system Hx = g.
For modern deep learning architectures, the Fisher Information Matrix H is an N \times N matrix where N is the number of network parameters. Explicitly computing, storing, and inverting this matrix is computationally intractable.
This is where the conjugate gradient (CG) method comes in. CG is an iterative algorithm for solving systems of linear equations like Hx = g without ever needing to explicitly construct the matrix H. The algorithm only requires the ability to compute matrix-vector products, specifically Hv for an arbitrary vector v.
This operation is called a Hessian-vector product (HVP). Using automatic differentiation frameworks, the HVP can be computed efficiently with two backward passes, requiring only slightly more computation than standard backpropagation:
Hv = \nabla_{\theta} \left( \left( \nabla_{\theta} \bar{D}_{KL}(\theta_{old}, \theta) \right)^T v \right)
By using the conjugate gradient method to estimate the search direction x, and then scaling it by the constraint scalar, TRPO achieves stable policy updates without the massive computational overhead of matrix inversion.


2.5 The Backtracking Algorithm
The reason TRPO needs a backtracking line search is that the math we just worked through relies heavily on local approximations. We used a first-order Taylor expansion for the objective function and a second-order approximation for the KL divergence.
To bridge the gap between the quadratic approximation and the true non-linear reality of the neural network, TRPO uses the backtracking line search. It evaluates the exact functions to guarantee the step is strictly beneficial.
Here is the step-by-step mechanics of the search:

Calculate the maximal proposed parameter update using the direction and scalar we derived earlier:
\Delta \theta = \sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{x^T H x}} x
Define a decay coefficient \alpha \in (0, 1), often set to 0.5, and initialize a decay index j = 0.
Propose a new set of policy parameters by taking a exponentially decaying fraction of the maximal step:
\theta_{new} = \theta_{old} + \alpha^j \Delta \theta
Evaluate this proposed \theta_{new} against two strict acceptance criteria using the true, unapproximated functions:
Objective improvement: L(\theta_{new}) > L(\theta_{old})
KL constraint boundary: D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}} \parallel \pi_{\theta_{new}}) \le \delta
If both conditions are satisfied, the search successfully terminates, and \theta_{new} is accepted as the new policy.
If either condition fails, it means the local approximation was too aggressive and overshot the safe region. The algorithm increments j by 1 (which shrinks the step size by another factor of \alpha) and repeats the evaluation.



2.6 Bridging the Gap with the Surrogate Objective
To understand why we can optimize a surrogate objective L(\theta) instead of the true expected return J(\theta), we need to look at their first derivatives. The foundational trick of TRPO is proving that at the exact point of the current policy parameters \theta_{old}, the gradient of the surrogate perfectly matches the gradient of the true objective.
Let’s define our terms formally:

\pi_\theta(a|s): The policy parameterized by \theta.
\theta_{old}: The current parameters of our policy before the update.
\rho_{\theta_{old}}(s): The state visitation distribution under the old policy.
A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a): The advantage function evaluated under the old policy.

First, we recall the standard Policy Gradient Theorem for our true objective J(\theta). Evaluated at the current parameters \theta_{old}, it is written as:
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
Next, we define our surrogate objective L(\theta). This function uses importance sampling to evaluate a proposed new policy using the trajectories collected by the old policy:
L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \frac{\pi_\theta(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
Notice the fraction in the L(\theta) equation: \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)}. This is an importance sampling ratio. Because we do not know the state distribution for the proposed new policy \pi_\theta, TRPO evaluates the objective using the trajectories and state distribution already collected by the old policy \pi_{\theta_{old}}. The importance sampling ratio corrects for the fact that we are evaluating a new policy using data generated by an old one. It asks: if the new policy makes a good action more likely, how much should we increase the objective?
To find the gradient of this surrogate objective L(\theta), we take the derivative with respect to \theta. Because the expectation is taken over states and actions sampled from the old policy, the distribution over which we are taking the expectation is independent of the active variable \theta. This allows us to pass the gradient operator directly inside the expectation:
\nabla_\theta L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
Now, we evaluate this gradient at the exact point of our current parameters, setting \theta = \theta_{old}:
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}}}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
At this stage, we apply the standard log-derivative trick, which states that \nabla_x \log f(x) = \frac{\nabla_x f(x)}{f(x)}. If we apply this identity to our policy at the point \theta_{old}, we get:
\frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}}}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a|s)} = \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}}
Substituting this identity back into our expectation yields our final result:
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_{old}}, a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}} \left[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} A_{\theta_{old}}(s, a) \right]
This final equation is identical to the right-hand side of the Policy Gradient Theorem. Therefore, we have proven:
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}} = \nabla_\theta J(\theta)|_{\theta = \theta_{old}}
Because their first derivatives match, taking a small step to maximize the easy-to-calculate surrogate L(\theta) guarantees we are moving in the exact same direction as if we were maximizing the impossible-to-calculate true objective J(\theta). However, because this equality only holds strictly at \theta = \theta_{old}, we must introduce the trust region constraint to ensure we do not step too far away from this point of equivalence.


2.7 Why TRPO Uses the Fisher Information Matrix
When we use standard gradient descent to update a neural network, we are taking a step in Euclidean space. We change the parameters \theta by some small Euclidean distance \Delta \theta.
However, a neural network policy \pi_\theta(a|s) outputs a probability distribution. The relationship between the parameters and the output distribution is highly non-linear. In some regions of the parameter space, a massive change in \theta might barely affect the output probabilities. In other regions, a microscopic change in \theta might drastically shift the probabilities, completely changing the agent’s behavior and destroying the policy.
If we define our trust region simply by limiting the Euclidean distance \Delta \theta^T \Delta \theta < \epsilon, we are ignoring the actual effect on the policy. Standard gradient descent does not understand the underlying geometry of the probability distributions it is creating.
The Fisher Information Matrix solves this problem by acting as a metric tensor for probability distributions. It defines the local geometry of the probability space, often referred to as a Riemannian manifold.
Instead of measuring the Euclidean distance between parameter vectors, we want to measure the statistical distance between the resulting probability distributions. The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence does exactly this.
If we look at the second-order Taylor expansion of the KL divergence between a policy and a slightly updated policy, a beautiful mathematical property emerges. The Hessian matrix (the matrix of second derivatives) of the KL divergence evaluated at the current parameters is exactly equal to the Fisher Information Matrix, which we will denote as F:
D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta} \parallel \pi_{\theta + \Delta \theta}) \approx \frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T F \Delta \theta
The FIM translates a change in parameters (\Delta \theta) into the resulting change in the probability distribution. By incorporating the FIM, TRPO transforms the standard gradient into the natural gradient. This ensures the algorithm takes steps of a consistent size in the actual behavior space, moving safely regardless of how the neural network parameters are parameterized.
TRPO explicitly substitutes the FIM into its optimization constraint to enforce the trust region. Recall the quadratic program TRPO attempts to solve. It maximizes the surrogate advantage g^T \Delta \theta subject to the KL divergence constraint. Using the relationship established above, TRPO mathematically frames the constraint using the FIM:
\frac{1}{2} \Delta \theta^T F \Delta \theta \le \delta
As derived earlier using Lagrange multipliers, the optimal step direction x for this constrained problem requires inverting this matrix:
x = F^{-1} g
This vector x is the natural gradient direction. It points toward the steepest improvement in the objective function while accounting for the curvature of the probability space defined by F.
Because the FIM is an N \times N matrix where N is the number of network parameters, explicitly constructing and inverting F is impossible for deep neural networks. TRPO uses the conjugate gradient method to approximate the solution to Fx = g. In this process, TRPO never builds the full FIM. Instead, it computes Fisher-vector products (Fv) for arbitrary vectors v.
Mathematically, the FIM is also defined as the expected outer product of the score function (the gradient of the log-probability):
F = \mathbb{E}_{s,a} \left[ \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s) \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)^T \right]
By leveraging automatic differentiation packages, TRPO can compute the product of this massive matrix and a vector v efficiently using a sequence of vector-Jacobian products, providing the precise directional curvature needed for the natural gradient step without the impossible memory requirements.


2.8 The Monotonic Improvement Guarantee
We established that maximizing the surrogate objective L(\theta) is equivalent to maximizing the true objective J(\theta) exactly at the current parameters \theta_{old}. However, as the new policy \pi_\theta diverges from \pi_{\theta_{old}}, this approximation breaks down. If we take too large a step, an increase in L(\theta) might actually result in a catastrophic decrease in the true expected return.
To prevent this, Schulman et al. derived a theoretical lower bound that strictly bounds the difference between the true objective and the surrogate objective. They proved that the true expected return is mathematically guaranteed to be greater than or equal to the surrogate objective minus a penalty based on how much the policy distribution changes.
The theoretical lower bound is defined as:
J(\theta) \ge L(\theta) - C \max_s D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_\theta(\cdot|s))
Let’s break down the components of this inequality:

J(\theta): The true expected return of the proposed new policy.
L(\theta): The surrogate objective evaluated using the old policy’s state distribution, \rho_{\theta_{old}}(s).
\max_s D_{KL}(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(\cdot|s) \parallel \pi_\theta(\cdot|s)): The maximum Kullback-Leibler divergence between the old and new policy across all possible states s.
C: A theoretical penalty coefficient defined as C = \frac{4\epsilon \gamma}{(1-\gamma)^2}, where \epsilon is the maximum absolute advantage and \gamma is the discount factor.

This equation is the mathematical bedrock of Trust Region Policy Optimization. It provides an absolute safety net. If we can find a new policy \theta that maximizes the right-hand side of this inequality, we are mathematically guaranteed that the true objective J(\theta) on the left-hand side will improve by at least that same amount.
By forcing the optimization process to consider the KL divergence penalty, the algorithm is mathematically prevented from taking a step that destroys the policy. It guarantees monotonic improvement.

title: PPO Series 2: Trust Region Policy Optimization
section: 3 From Natural Policy Gradient to Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
3 From Natural Policy Gradient to Trust Region Policy Optimization
Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) is fundamentally an extension and practical stabilization of the Natural Policy Gradient (NPG) algorithm (Kakade 2001). While they share the exact same underlying philosophy regarding the geometry of probability space, TRPO solves a critical flaw in how NPG applies its updates.
Both NPG and TRPO recognize that standard gradient descent is flawed for updating policies. Taking a step of a fixed Euclidean distance in parameter space can lead to wildly unpredictable changes in the actual probability distribution of the policy.
To fix this, both algorithms calculate the exact same update direction. They multiply the standard policy gradient g by the inverse of the Fisher Information Matrix F:
x = F^{-1} g
This vector x is the natural gradient. It points in the direction of steepest objective improvement while accounting for the curvature of the probability manifold.

3.1 Where NPG Falls Short: The Step Size Problem
The original Natural Policy Gradient algorithm uses this natural gradient direction but relies on a standard, fixed learning rate (or step size) \alpha:
\theta_{new} = \theta_{old} + \alpha F^{-1} g
This is where NPG runs into practical problems. Because the curvature of the probability space changes dynamically as the neural network learns, a fixed learning rate is incredibly unstable. In some states, a specific \alpha might result in a tiny, inefficient step. In other states, that exact same \alpha might result in a massive jump that completely destroys the policy’s behavior. NPG provides no mathematical guarantees against taking a destructive step.


3.2 How TRPO Extends NPG: The Trust Region
TRPO can be viewed as NPG augmented with a mathematically rigorous step-size calculation. It takes the natural gradient direction from NPG but completely replaces the fixed learning rate with a dynamic scalar derived from a hard Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence constraint.
Instead of guessing a safe learning rate \alpha, TRPO asks the user to define \delta, the maximum allowed change in the probability distribution. By enforcing the constraint D_{KL} \le \delta, TRPO analytically calculates the exact maximum step size that can be taken in the natural gradient direction without violating the trust region:
\Delta \theta = \sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{x^T F x}} x


3.3 The Line Search Guarantee
Furthermore, because both the natural gradient and the analytical step size rely on local Taylor approximations, TRPO adds a backtracking line search, which NPG lacks. The line search evaluates the true, unapproximated non-linear objective function and the exact KL divergence to ensure the proposed natural gradient step is strictly beneficial.
In summary, NPG defines the mathematically optimal direction to update a probability distribution, while TRPO provides the mechanical constraints and safety checks required to stably walk in that direction when using deep neural networks.

title: PPO Series 2: Trust Region Policy Optimization
section: 4 Second-Order Taylor Expansion of the KL Divergence
text:
4 Second-Order Taylor Expansion of the KL Divergence
To derive this approximation, we need to perform a Taylor expansion of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence function around the current policy parameters \theta_{old}.
For clarity in the derivation, let p_\theta(x) represent our parameterized probability distribution, which corresponds to the policy \pi_\theta(a|s) in reinforcement learning.
The KL divergence between the old distribution and the new distribution is defined as:
D_{KL}(p_{\theta_{old}} \parallel p_\theta) = \sum_x p_{\theta_{old}}(x) \log \frac{p_{\theta_{old}}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}
Let f(\theta) = D_{KL}(p_{\theta_{old}} \parallel p_\theta). We want to approximate f(\theta) at a point \theta = \theta_{old} + \Delta\theta.
The general formula for a second-order multivariate Taylor expansion of f(\theta) around \theta_{old} is:
f(\theta) \approx f(\theta_{old}) + \nabla_\theta f(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}}^T \Delta\theta + \frac{1}{2} \Delta\theta^T \nabla^2_\theta f(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}} \Delta\theta
We will evaluate each of these three terms individually.
The zeroth-order term is simply the function evaluated at \theta_{old}:
f(\theta_{old}) = D_{KL}(p_{\theta_{old}} \parallel p_{\theta_{old}})
By definition, the KL divergence between two identical distributions is exactly zero. Mathematically:
D_{KL}(p_{\theta_{old}} \parallel p_{\theta_{old}}) = \sum_x p_{\theta_{old}}(x) \log \frac{p_{\theta_{old}}(x)}{p_{\theta_{old}}(x)} = \sum_x p_{\theta_{old}}(x) \log(1) = 0
Next, we calculate the gradient of the KL divergence with respect to the new parameters \theta:
\nabla_\theta f(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \left( \sum_x p_{\theta_{old}}(x) \left( \log p_{\theta_{old}}(x) - \log p_\theta(x) \right) \right)
Because p_{\theta_{old}}(x) is a constant with respect to \theta, its derivative is zero. We can move the gradient operator inside the summation:
\nabla_\theta f(\theta) = - \sum_x p_{\theta_{old}}(x) \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x)
Here, we apply the log-derivative trick, which states that \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) = \frac{\nabla_\theta p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(x)}:
\nabla_\theta f(\theta) = - \sum_x p_{\theta_{old}}(x) \frac{\nabla_\theta p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(x)}
Now, we must evaluate this gradient at the point \theta = \theta_{old} to find the first-order coefficient for our Taylor expansion:
\nabla_\theta f(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}} = - \sum_x p_{\theta_{old}}(x) \frac{\nabla_\theta p_\theta(x)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}}}{p_{\theta_{old}}(x)}
The p_{\theta_{old}}(x) terms in the numerator and denominator cancel out:
\nabla_\theta f(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}} = - \sum_x \nabla_\theta p_\theta(x)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}}
Because the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, we can pull the gradient operator outside the summation:
\nabla_\theta f(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}} = - \nabla_\theta \left( \sum_x p_\theta(x) \right)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}}
A fundamental property of any valid probability distribution is that all its probabilities must sum to 1. Therefore, \sum_x p_\theta(x) = 1.
\nabla_\theta f(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}} = - \nabla_\theta (1) = 0
Because the derivative of a constant is zero, the entire first-order term vanishes.
Since the zeroth-order and first-order terms are both exactly zero, the Taylor expansion relies entirely on the second-order term.
Let H denote the Hessian matrix (the matrix of second derivatives) of the KL divergence evaluated at \theta_{old}:
H = \nabla^2_\theta f(\theta)|_{\theta=\theta_{old}}
Substituting H into the second-order term of the Taylor polynomial gives us the final approximation:
D_{KL}(p_{\theta_{old}} \parallel p_\theta) \approx 0 + 0 + \frac{1}{2} \Delta\theta^T H \Delta\theta
This confirms that for small updates, the KL divergence is approximated purely by a quadratic penalty scaled by the Hessian matrix.

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
text:
Most LLM applications still treat the agent as an extension of the chat loop. OpenClaw starts from a different premise: once an agent becomes persistent, tool-using, and multi-surface, the real problem is no longer prompt formatting but runtime design.
That shift is what makes OpenClaw interesting. It is not an operating system in the kernel sense. But it is an always-on agent runtime centered on a Gateway control plane, and it can be usefully understood as an agent-OS-like layer running above the host OS. Rather than optimizing for chat UX first, it shifts the center of gravity toward a persistent runtime: a Gateway that maintains provider connections, exposes a typed WebSocket API, and serves as the shared control plane for clients and nodes across surfaces.
When agents run for multiple steps, the main challenge is no longer just prompting. It becomes a runtime problem: how to route messages, serialize execution, stream tool output coherently, preserve session state, and keep the system operable across multiple interfaces. OpenClaw approaches these concerns as infrastructure problems rather than as prompt-design problems. In that architecture, chat is not the whole system; it is one surface among several, alongside the CLI, web UI, macOS app, and connected nodes.
Capability expansion is handled through skills. OpenClaw snapshots eligible skills when a session starts and reuses that list across turns in the same session for performance. When the skills watcher is enabled, or when a newly eligible remote node appears, that skill list can refresh mid-session and be picked up on the next agent turn.
Compared with dialogue-centered agent setups, OpenClaw looks less like a chat wrapper and more like an operational runtime. The distinctive point is not merely that it can call tools, but that connectivity, session execution, queueing, routing, and tool dispatch are all organized behind a single control plane.

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
section: 2 A von Neumann Metaphor for Agent Systems
text:
2 A von Neumann Metaphor for Agent Systems
The best way to understand this shift is as an architectural metaphor. OpenClaw does not implement a kernel, but it does assume a set of OS-like responsibilities at the agent layer: control, I/O coordination, state continuity, execution governance, and bounded tool access.
At the center sits the Gateway, which functions as both controller and bus. It owns messaging surfaces, accepts WebSocket connections from clients and nodes, validates frames, emits typed events, and uses a structured handshake in which role, device identity, and capabilities are declared up front. That gives OpenClaw a unified control plane for routing, pairing, presence, and command flow across interfaces.
Within that system, the LLM plays the role of the general-purpose inference engine. It is the component that plans, selects tools, and generates responses, while the Gateway and runtime provide the scaffolding that keeps those actions connected to sessions, channels, tools, and policy boundaries. OpenClaw explicitly treats the agent as a managed session with lifecycle control, event handling, prompt customization, persistence, compaction, and model switching.
The memory hierarchy is likewise layered, though only metaphorically. The immediate model context acts like short-term working state; the session runtime preserves active continuity for the turn; and longer-lived workspace files, session artifacts, and diagnostics provide durable state on disk. OpenClaw’s design makes the durable layer unusually explicit by storing memory in Markdown files inside the workspace and treating those files as canonical.
The interfaces around that runtime—CLI, web UI, WebChat, macOS app, and nodes—function like multiplexed I/O surfaces attached to the same computational system. They are not isolated assistants with separate brains; they are different entry points into a shared Gateway-managed runtime.
To expand capabilities, OpenClaw uses skills as modular runtime extensions. Skills are loaded into the session environment and prompt, can be bundled, managed, or workspace-based, and can refresh dynamically under documented conditions. This makes capability growth more composable than relying entirely on one large, hardcoded prompt.
Finally, tools and nodes—local files, browser control, shell execution, APIs, camera, screen recording, location, and other commands—form the agent’s operational environment. OpenClaw’s important move is not simply that the agent can reach those tools, but that access is brought under a common runtime model with pairing, approval, queueing, sandbox options, typed events, and logging.

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
section: 3 The Agentic Loop as a Managed Execution Lifecycle

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
section: 4 Memory and State: Local-First, File-Backed, Auditable
text:
4 Memory and State: Local-First, File-Backed, Auditable
When people build agents, the instinct is often to start with a vector database. OpenClaw takes a more systems-first approach: memory is local-first, file-backed, and human-auditable, while semantic retrieval is layered on top of canonical files rather than replacing them. Memory is plain Markdown in the agent workspace, and those files are the source of truth.

4.1 Markdown-on-Disk as the Source of Truth
OpenClaw memory lives in workspace files, not in an opaque memory service. The model only “remembers” what gets written to disk. This design makes state inspectable, editable, and diffable by ordinary filesystem tools. In practice, it also makes the workspace easy to back up and version.


4.2 Separating Identity from Episodic Memory
OpenClaw also separates bootstrap identity and operating context from recall-oriented memory. In the workspace, it expects user-editable files such as AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, TOOLS.md, IDENTITY.md, and USER.md; during session startup, the template flow directs the agent to read SOUL.md, USER.md, recent daily memory, and, in the main session, MEMORY.md. This creates a practical distinction between always-present operating context and selectively accumulated memory.


4.3 Privacy Boundaries as a First-Class Rule
That separation is paired with an explicit privacy rule. MEMORY.md, the curated long-term memory file, is loaded only in the main private session and never in group contexts. This materially reduces the chance that long-term personal context is injected into shared channels by default.


4.4 Vector Search is a Derived Capability
OpenClaw does support semantic and hybrid retrieval, but the retrieval layer is deliberately downstream of the files themselves. The memory plugin provides search and retrieval functions, and the system supports hybrid search, reranking, temporal weighting, and optional vector acceleration. The important design point is that the index is derived from Markdown rather than replacing Markdown as the canonical store.


4.5 Pluggable Retrieval Backends
Because the files remain canonical, OpenClaw can vary the retrieval backend without changing the memory format. That keeps storage and retrieval decoupled and makes the system more operable for teams that care about inspectability over black-box persistence.
This memory design is one of OpenClaw’s clearest systems choices. Critical identity and behavioral context live in explicit workspace files; episodic and durable recall live in Markdown memory layers; and semantic retrieval is an optional acceleration layer rather than the core substrate.
That tradeoff is significant. It favors inspectability and operational trust over the illusion of “magical memory,” which is often harder to debug, harder to govern, and harder to recover when things go wrong.

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
text:
5 Conclusion
The shift from a conversational wrapper to a runtime-centric design is not merely aesthetic. OpenClaw centralizes connectivity through the Gateway, serializes agent execution by session lane, exposes queue modes that can steer or defer input, and anchors longer-lived memory in auditable workspace files. Together, those choices target the operational friction that appears once agents become persistent, tool-using, and multi-surface.
Just as importantly, this runtime discipline creates cleaner operational traces. Because OpenClaw separates lifecycle events, assistant output, tool events, queueing behavior, session state, and usage telemetry, it appears well suited to collecting structured agent trajectories. That does not mean the project officially positions itself as an RLHF or post-training framework; rather, it suggests that OpenClaw provides a promising substrate for future preference-learning or reinforcement-learning-style work on end-to-end agent behavior.
Frameworks remain excellent for prototyping agent logic. But operating agents across real tools, real sessions, and real interfaces requires governance, observability, and state you can actually inspect. OpenClaw’s significance is that it pushes those concerns into the runtime itself and treats them as first-class system design problems.
